courseTitle: AI Automation & Chatbot VA: From Zero to First Client
courseDescription: A complete beginner-to-job-ready training program for aspiring AI Automation & Chatbot Virtual Assistants. Covers Zapier and Make, connecting AI to automations, building FAQ chatbots, mapping and documenting client workflows, portfolio-building, resume and proposal writing, and how to land and manage your first automation client.
priceNote: One-time payment unlocks lifetime access to all modules, video lessons, quizzes, and your Certificate of Completion.

modules.title: Module 1: Starting Out as an AI Automation VA

lessons.title: What Is an AI Automation VA?

slides.heading: What Is an AI Automation VA?
bullets: Welcome to your AI Automation VA journey
Builds workflows that connect apps and remove manual work
A specialist within the broader AI-Powered VA world
slides.narration: Welcome to Module 1 of your AI Automation & Chatbot VA training. An AI Automation VA designs and builds workflows - using tools like Zapier, Make, and simple AI-powered chatbots - that connect a business's different apps together so information moves automatically instead of being copied and pasted by hand.

slides.heading: What an AI Automation VA Actually Does Day to Day
bullets: Maps out a client's repetitive task step by step
Builds and tests the automation in Zapier or Make
Sets up simple chatbots to handle common questions
slides.narration: On a typical day, an AI Automation VA might interview a client about a repetitive task, map it out step by step, build and test the actual automation, and set up or refine a simple chatbot that answers a business's most common customer questions automatically.

slides.heading: Why Businesses Hire a Dedicated Automation Specialist
bullets: Automation tools have a real learning curve
A broken or badly-built automation can cause real problems
Business owners want it built right the first time
slides.narration: While automation tools like Zapier look simple on the surface, building something reliable that won't quietly break or send the wrong information takes real skill - business owners hire a dedicated Automation VA so it gets built correctly and keeps working.

slides.heading: Is This Niche Right for You?
bullets: You enjoy logical, step-by-step problem solving
You're patient enough to test things thoroughly
You like the satisfaction of 'set it and forget it' systems
slides.narration: This niche is a great fit if you enjoy breaking a messy process down into clear logical steps, if you have the patience to test an automation thoroughly before handing it over, and if you find real satisfaction in building a system that quietly keeps working long after you built it.

lessons.title: Skills and Traits of a Great Automation VA

slides.heading: Core Skills You'll Build
bullets: Workflow mapping - turning a messy process into clear steps
Hands-on Zapier and Make building
Testing and troubleshooting broken automations
slides.narration: Over this training, you'll build three core skills: mapping a real business process into clear, logical steps, building that process hands-on in Zapier and Make, and testing and troubleshooting when something doesn't work exactly as planned.

slides.heading: Traits Clients Look For
bullets: Thoroughness - testing every likely scenario
Clear documentation of what was built and why
Honesty about what automation can't fix
slides.narration: Clients trust Automation VAs who thoroughly test an automation before calling it done, who document clearly what was built and how it works, and who are honest when a task genuinely needs a human touch rather than forcing a bad automation onto it.

slides.heading: A Day in the Life
bullets: Morning: check that yesterday's automations ran correctly
Midday: build or refine a new workflow
End of day: document changes and note any issues
slides.narration: A typical day might start by checking that every automation ran correctly overnight, move into building or refining a new workflow for a client, and end with documenting any changes made and flagging anything that needs a closer look tomorrow.

slides.heading: Where Growth Leads
bullets: Handle more complex, multi-step workflows over time
Move into building smarter chatbots with AI built in
Manage a portfolio of automations across several clients
slides.narration: As you gain experience, you can grow from simple single-trigger automations into complex multi-step workflows, add real AI intelligence into your chatbots and automations, and eventually manage a whole portfolio of running systems across multiple clients.

lessons.title: How Businesses Actually Waste Time (and Where Automation Helps)

slides.heading: The Hidden Cost of Manual Repetition
bullets: Small repeated tasks add up to real hours every week
Manual copy-paste work is where errors creep in
Owners rarely realize how much time it actually costs
slides.narration: A five-minute task repeated ten times a day adds up to hours every single week - and manual, repetitive copy-paste work is exactly where typos and missed steps creep in. Most business owners have never actually added up what it's costing them.

slides.heading: Common Time-Wasting Patterns to Look For
bullets: Re-typing the same information into multiple places
Manually notifying people when something happens
Answering the same customer questions over and over
slides.narration: Watch for these common patterns: information being re-typed into multiple systems by hand, someone manually messaging a teammate every time an event happens, and customer service reps answering the exact same questions again and again.

slides.heading: Spotting an Automation Opportunity in a Conversation
bullets: Listen for 'every time X happens, I have to...'
Listen for 'I always forget to...'
Listen for 'my team keeps mixing this up'
slides.narration: In any conversation with a business owner, listen for phrases like "every time a new order comes in, I have to..." or "I always forget to follow up on..." - these are direct signals pointing to a specific, buildable automation opportunity.

slides.heading: Ready for Module 2
bullets: You understand where automation actually helps
You can spot opportunities in a real conversation
Next: the specific tools you'll build with
slides.narration: You now understand what an AI Automation VA does and how to spot real opportunities in a business's day-to-day work. In Module 2, we'll get hands-on with the specific tools you'll use to actually build these workflows.

lessons.title: Setting Up Your Automation Workspace & Tools Checklist

slides.heading: What You Actually Need to Get Started
bullets: A laptop or desktop with a modern browser
Free accounts on Zapier and Make to start practicing
A simple diagramming tool or even just pen and paper
slides.narration: You don't need expensive software to start - a reliable computer, free accounts on Zapier and Make (both offer usable free tiers for learning), and even just pen and paper for sketching out workflows is enough to begin practicing.

slides.heading: Organizing Your Automation Library
bullets: Save a plain-language map of every workflow you build
Note which apps and triggers were used
Build this into a reusable template library
slides.narration: Keep a running library of every workflow you build, saved as a plain-language map noting which apps, triggers, and actions were used - over time, many new client requests turn out to be small variations of something you've already built.

slides.heading: Understanding Free vs Paid Automation Plans
bullets: Free tiers are enough to learn and build simple flows
Paid tiers unlock more tasks per month and premium apps
Always clarify upfront who pays for the client's plan
slides.narration: Free tiers of Zapier and Make are genuinely enough to learn on and build simple automations, while paid tiers unlock a higher monthly task limit and connections to premium apps - always clarify upfront whether you or the client covers any subscription cost for their live automation.

slides.heading: Ready for Module 2
bullets: You know what the role involves
You have a basic toolkit ready
Next: mastering the tools themselves
slides.narration: You now understand what an AI Automation VA does and have the basics ready to start practicing. In Module 2, we'll dive deep into the specific platforms you'll be building with every day.

modules.title: Module 2: Essential Automation Tools Every AI Automation VA Must Know

lessons.title: Zapier Deep Dive: Triggers, Actions, and Multi-Step Zaps

slides.heading: The Anatomy of a Zap
bullets: Trigger - the event that starts everything
Action(s) - what happens in response
Multi-step Zaps chain several actions together
slides.narration: Every Zap starts with a trigger - a specific event like a new form submission - followed by one or more actions that happen in response. A multi-step Zap simply chains several actions together, so one trigger can update a spreadsheet, send a message, and create a task all at once.

slides.heading: Filters and Paths
bullets: Filters stop a Zap unless a condition is met
Paths let a Zap branch in different directions
Both add real logic to a simple trigger-action flow
slides.narration: Filters let you stop a Zap from continuing unless a specific condition is true - for example, only notify the team if an order is over a certain amount. Paths let a single Zap branch into different directions depending on the data, adding real decision-making logic.

slides.heading: Formatter and Data Cleanup
bullets: Raw data often needs reformatting before use
Zapier's Formatter step cleans dates, text, and numbers
A small cleanup step prevents many downstream errors
slides.narration: Data coming from one app is often in the wrong format for another - a date written differently, extra spaces in a name. Zapier's built-in Formatter step cleans this up mid-workflow, and skipping this step is one of the most common causes of an automation quietly breaking.

slides.heading: When Zapier Is (and Isn't) the Right Tool
bullets: Great for simple, linear, single-path automations
Gets harder to manage with heavy branching logic
Know when it's time to consider Make instead
slides.narration: Zapier is the right tool for simple, mostly linear automations with a clear trigger and predictable actions. Once a workflow needs heavy branching, loops, or complex logic, it's worth considering Make instead - which we'll cover next.

lessons.title: Make (Integromat) Deep Dive: Modules, Routers, and Filters

slides.heading: Why Make Handles Complexity Better
bullets: Visual, flowchart-style scenario builder
Built for branching, looping, and complex logic
Steeper learning curve, but far more powerful
slides.narration: Make's visual, flowchart-style builder lets you see an entire workflow ('scenario') laid out at once, and it's built from the ground up to handle branching, looping, and complex logic that would be awkward to force into a simpler tool.

slides.heading: Modules and Routers
bullets: Each step in Make is called a module
A router splits one flow into multiple branches
Each branch can have its own filter conditions
slides.narration: In Make, each individual step is called a module, and a router lets one incoming flow split into multiple branches - each branch can carry its own filter conditions, so different types of data get handled completely differently within the same scenario.

slides.heading: Error Handling in Make
bullets: Scenarios can be set to retry on failure
Error handlers catch and respond to specific failures
Critical for automations that must never silently fail
slides.narration: Make lets you configure a scenario to automatically retry a failed step, and dedicated error handlers can catch specific failures and respond appropriately - for example, notifying you directly rather than letting a broken automation fail silently for days.

slides.heading: Choosing Zapier vs Make for a Client
bullets: Simple, one-path task: Zapier is faster to build
Complex, multi-branch logic: Make is more reliable
Many Automation VAs end up using both
slides.narration: For a simple, one-path task, Zapier is usually faster to build and easier for a client to understand later. For genuinely complex, multi-branch logic, Make tends to be more reliable long-term - most working Automation VAs end up comfortable with both.

lessons.title: Connecting AI to Automations (ChatGPT + Zapier/Make)

slides.heading: Why Add AI Into an Automation
bullets: Automations move data - AI can also think about it
Draft a reply, summarize, or categorize automatically
Turns a simple data pipe into a smart assistant
slides.narration: A plain automation moves data from one place to another, but adding an AI step lets it also think about that data - drafting a reply, summarizing a long message, or categorizing an incoming request automatically before it reaches a human.

slides.heading: Using ChatGPT/OpenAI Steps in Zapier and Make
bullets: Both platforms have built-in AI/ChatGPT actions
Feed it the automation's data as the prompt
Pass its response into the next step
slides.narration: Both Zapier and Make have built-in AI actions that can call ChatGPT or similar models directly inside a workflow - you feed it the data flowing through the automation as part of the prompt, and pass its response straight into the next step.

slides.heading: A Practical Example: Auto-Categorizing Support Emails
bullets: New email comes in as the trigger
AI step reads it and picks a category
Automation routes it to the right person or folder
slides.narration: A practical example: a new support email triggers the automation, an AI step reads it and decides which category it falls into (billing, technical, general), and the automation then routes it to the right person or folder automatically - no manual sorting required.

slides.heading: Keeping AI Steps Reliable
bullets: Give the AI step a very specific, constrained prompt
Always have a fallback for an unexpected AI response
Test with real, messy examples before going live
slides.narration: Keep the AI step's prompt specific and constrained ("reply with exactly one of these three words") rather than open-ended, always build in a fallback path for an unexpected response, and test with real, messy examples before ever turning it on for a live client.

lessons.title: No-Code Chatbot Builders (Voiceflow, Chatbase, Custom GPTs)

slides.heading: What a No-Code Chatbot Builder Gives You
bullets: A visual way to design conversation flows
No programming required to launch a working bot
Connects to a business's own documents or FAQs
slides.narration: No-code chatbot builders let you visually design a conversation flow - what the bot says, what it asks, how it branches - without writing any code, and many can be trained directly on a business's own FAQ document or website content.

slides.heading: Chatbase and Similar Document-Trained Bots
bullets: Upload a business's FAQs or help docs
The bot answers using only that information
Fast way to launch a useful support chatbot
slides.narration: Tools like Chatbase let you upload a business's existing FAQ page or help documents, and the resulting chatbot answers customer questions using only that information - this is often the fastest way to launch a genuinely useful support chatbot.

slides.heading: Voiceflow for More Designed Conversations
bullets: Visual conversation-flow builder, like a flowchart for chat
Good for structured processes - booking, intake forms
More control than a pure document-trained bot
slides.narration: Voiceflow is built for designing more structured conversations step by step, like a flowchart - well suited to processes like appointment booking or an intake questionnaire where the exact flow of questions matters.

slides.heading: Custom GPTs as a Simple Chatbot Option
bullets: ChatGPT's own custom GPT builder needs no code either
Good for internal tools or simple public-facing bots
Easiest option if a client already uses ChatGPT Plus
slides.narration: OpenAI's own custom GPT builder is a genuinely no-code option too, and it's often the simplest choice if a client is already comfortable with ChatGPT - well suited to internal team tools or a straightforward public-facing FAQ bot.

lessons.title: Webhooks, APIs, and Google Sheets/Forms as Building Blocks

slides.heading: What a Webhook Actually Is
bullets: A way for one app to instantly notify another
Triggers an automation the moment something happens
You don't need to write code to use one
slides.narration: A webhook is simply a way for one app to instantly notify another the moment something happens - it's what lets an automation trigger immediately rather than checking every few minutes. Zapier and Make both let you use webhooks without writing any code.

slides.heading: What an API Is, in Plain Terms
bullets: A standard way apps talk to each other
Automation platforms handle the technical part for you
You mostly just need to know an API connection exists
slides.narration: An API is just a standard way for two pieces of software to exchange information - as an Automation VA using Zapier or Make, the platform handles the technical connection for you; you mainly need to know that a given app has an API connection available at all.

slides.heading: Google Sheets and Forms as Your Simplest Building Blocks
bullets: A spreadsheet as a lightweight database
Google Forms as an easy, free data-collection trigger
Great starting point for almost any small business
slides.narration: Google Sheets works surprisingly well as a lightweight database for small automations, and Google Forms is a free, easy way to collect structured data that can trigger a workflow - together they're often the simplest, cheapest starting point for a small business's first automation.

slides.heading: Putting the Building Blocks Together
bullets: Form submission -> webhook or native trigger
Data cleaned and logged to a spreadsheet
AI step and notification action complete the flow
slides.narration: A complete simple system might look like: a Google Form submission triggers the automation, the data gets cleaned and logged to a spreadsheet, an AI step drafts a response, and a final action sends a notification - each block simple on its own, powerful together.

modules.title: Module 3: Core Automation & Chatbot Building Skills

lessons.title: Mapping a Client's Workflow Before Automating It

slides.heading: Why Mapping Comes Before Building
bullets: Building first often means rebuilding later
A clear map catches edge cases early
Takes minutes, saves hours
slides.narration: Jumping straight into Zapier before mapping the workflow almost always means rebuilding parts of it later - spending a few minutes mapping the process in plain language first catches edge cases and missing steps before they become a broken automation.

slides.heading: Interviewing a Client About Their Process
bullets: Ask them to walk through it exactly as they do it today
Ask 'what happens if...' for every likely exception
Watch a screen-share if possible - people forget steps
slides.narration: Ask the client to walk through the process exactly as they do it today, step by step, and ask "what happens if..." for every exception you can think of. If possible, watch a screen-share of them doing it once - people reliably forget small steps when just describing it verbally.

slides.heading: Turning a Conversation Into a Simple Flowchart
bullets: Boxes for each step, arrows for what happens next
Diamonds for any yes/no decision points
Even a rough sketch is enough to build from
slides.narration: Turn the conversation into a simple flowchart: a box for each step, arrows showing what happens next, and a diamond shape for any yes/no decision point - even a rough hand-drawn version is enough to build the actual automation from confidently.

slides.heading: Confirming the Map Before Building
bullets: Walk the map back to the client in plain language
Get their explicit confirmation it's accurate
Saves you from building the wrong thing
slides.narration: Before opening any automation tool, walk the finished map back to the client in plain language and get their explicit confirmation that it's accurate - this single step prevents the most expensive mistake in this niche: building the wrong thing correctly.

lessons.title: Building Your First Multi-Step Automation End-to-End

slides.heading: Starting With the Trigger
bullets: Pick the most reliable trigger available
Test it fires correctly before adding anything else
A shaky trigger undermines everything built on it
slides.narration: Always start by setting up and testing the trigger alone - firing it a few times to confirm it reliably detects the right event - before adding a single action on top of it. A shaky, unreliable trigger will undermine everything you build afterward.

slides.heading: Adding Actions One at a Time
bullets: Build and test one action, then add the next
Confirm the data passed between steps looks correct
Resist the urge to build all steps before testing any
slides.narration: Add and test one action at a time rather than building the entire multi-step flow before testing anything - check that the data passed from each step to the next actually looks correct, since this is where most silent errors hide.

slides.heading: Handling the Edge Cases You Mapped Earlier
bullets: Go back to your workflow map's exception list
Build a filter or path for each one
An automation that only handles the 'happy path' isn't done
slides.narration: Return to the exceptions you identified while mapping the workflow, and build a specific filter or path for each one - an automation that only works when everything goes perfectly isn't actually finished yet.

slides.heading: Final Review Before Going Live
bullets: Run it end-to-end with real, messy test data
Have the client review the actual result, not just the plan
Turn it on only after their explicit sign-off
slides.narration: Run the finished automation end-to-end using real, messy sample data rather than a perfectly clean example, have the client review the actual result it produces, and only turn it on live after their explicit sign-off.

lessons.title: Designing a Simple FAQ Chatbot That Actually Helps

slides.heading: Starting From Real Questions, Not Guesses
bullets: Pull actual questions from past emails or chats
Group them into clear categories
Write the answer in the business's real voice
slides.narration: Build a chatbot's content from a business's real, historical customer questions - pulled from old emails or chat logs - rather than guessing what people might ask. Group similar questions together and write each answer in the business's actual voice.

slides.heading: Designing for the 'I Don't Know' Case
bullets: A bot will always get an unexpected question eventually
Never let it guess confidently when it doesn't know
Always offer a clear path to a human
slides.narration: Every chatbot will eventually get a question outside what it was trained to answer - design it to recognize this and say so honestly rather than guessing confidently, and always offer a clear, easy path to reach a real human instead.

slides.heading: Keeping the Bot's Tone On-Brand
bullets: Match the business's existing tone, not a generic bot voice
Short, clear answers beat long paragraphs in chat
Review actual sample conversations before launch
slides.narration: Write the bot's responses to match the business's existing tone rather than a generic, robotic chatbot voice, keep answers short and scannable since long paragraphs read poorly in a chat window, and review full sample conversations before launch, not just individual answers in isolation.

slides.heading: Launching and Improving Over Time
bullets: Start with your best-guess set of questions
Review real conversations after a few weeks
Add new answers based on what people actually ask
slides.narration: Launch with your best first version, then review real conversation logs after a few weeks - people will ask things you didn't anticipate, and steadily adding new answers based on real usage is how a chatbot actually improves over time.

lessons.title: Testing, Error-Handling, and Documenting What You Build

slides.heading: Testing Like Something Will Go Wrong
bullets: Test the happy path, then deliberately break it
Try missing fields, weird characters, duplicate entries
Assume real-world data will be messier than your test
slides.narration: Test the ideal scenario first, then deliberately try to break your own automation - missing form fields, unusual characters, duplicate submissions. Real-world data is reliably messier than whatever clean example you tested with initially.

slides.heading: Building in Error Notifications
bullets: Set up an alert for when a step fails
Send it somewhere you'll actually see quickly
Silent failures are far worse than obvious ones
slides.narration: Configure your automation platform to alert you the moment any step fails, sent somewhere you'll genuinely see quickly - a silent failure that runs undetected for days does far more damage to a client relationship than an obvious, quickly-fixed error.

slides.heading: Writing Documentation a Non-Technical Client Can Read
bullets: Plain-language summary of what it does
A simple diagram or step list
What to do if something looks wrong
slides.narration: Write a short, plain-language summary of what the automation does, paired with a simple diagram or numbered step list, and a short section on what the client should do (and who to contact) if something ever looks wrong.

slides.heading: Handing It Over Professionally
bullets: Walk the client through the documentation live
Confirm they know who maintains it going forward
Agree on how future changes get requested
slides.narration: Walk the client through the documentation together on a short call rather than just emailing it, confirm they understand who's responsible for maintaining it going forward, and agree clearly on how they should request any future changes.

lessons.title: Creating Mock Automation Projects

slides.heading: Why You Need Samples Before Your First Client
bullets: Clients want to see proof, not just a resume
A mock project shows your actual building process
You control the quality with no deadline pressure
slides.narration: Since you may not have a paying client yet, building a mock automation for a fictional or real local business lets you show proof of your skills, not just claim them on a resume - and you control the quality with no deadline pressure.

slides.heading: Picking a Realistic Practice Project
bullets: Choose a genuinely common small-business need
Lead intake, order confirmation, or review requests work well
Keep the scope small enough to finish and document well
slides.narration: Pick a genuinely common small-business need - automatically logging new leads, sending order confirmations, or requesting reviews after a purchase - and keep the scope small enough that you can finish it and document it thoroughly.

slides.heading: Documenting Your Process, Not Just the Result
bullets: Screenshot the workflow map and the final build
Write a short explanation of your approach
Include the actual tools, triggers, and logic used
slides.narration: Document the full process, not just the finished result: screenshot both your workflow map and the final automation build, and write a short explanation including the actual tools, triggers, and logic you used - exactly what a client wants to see.

slides.heading: Keeping It Honest
bullets: Label mock projects clearly as sample work
Never claim invented results as a real client's
Honesty about samples builds more trust than exaggeration
slides.narration: Always label mock projects clearly as sample or practice work rather than presenting them as real client results - being upfront about this builds far more trust with a future client than an impressive-sounding but fabricated case study ever would.

lessons.title: Building an Automation VA Portfolio

slides.heading: What an Automation Portfolio Needs
bullets: A short intro about you and your toolset
2-3 sample workflows with diagrams
Clear labeling of real vs sample work
slides.narration: A strong Automation VA portfolio has a short introduction about you and the specific tools you specialize in, two or three sample workflows shown with simple diagrams, and honest labeling throughout of what's real client work versus practice samples.

slides.heading: Showing the Workflow Visually
bullets: A simple before/after diagram works better than text alone
Screenshot the actual Zapier or Make build
Visuals make an abstract skill feel concrete
slides.narration: A simple before/after diagram - the messy manual process versus the new automated flow - communicates your value far faster than a paragraph of text, and a screenshot of the actual Zapier or Make build makes an abstract skill feel concrete and real.

slides.heading: Where to Host Your Portfolio
bullets: A simple free website (Carrd, Notion, or similar)
A well-organized Google Drive folder works too
Keep the link short and easy to share
slides.narration: You don't need a paid website - a simple free site built in Carrd or Notion, or even a neatly organized, view-only Google Drive folder, works perfectly well as long as the link is short and easy to drop into a proposal or message.

slides.heading: Keeping Your Portfolio Updated
bullets: Swap in real client work as soon as you have it
Add new tools and integrations as you learn them
Revisit it every few months as platforms evolve
slides.narration: As soon as you land real client work (with their permission to showcase it), swap it in for your mock samples, and keep adding new tools and integrations as you learn them - revisiting your portfolio every few months keeps it looking current.

lessons.title: Showing Time & Cost Saved as Your Core Result

slides.heading: Why Time and Cost Saved Convert Best
bullets: It's the clearest, most concrete automation metric
Clients hire outcomes, not tool familiarity
Even a modest, honest number builds real trust
slides.narration: Time and cost saved are the clearest, most concrete results an Automation VA can show - a specific number, even a modest one, builds trust far faster than a vague claim about being 'automation-savvy.'

slides.heading: What to Measure Before and After
bullets: Time the manual process honestly before building
Note the exact date the automation went live
Re-measure the new process a few weeks later
slides.narration: Time how long the manual process genuinely takes before you build anything, note the exact date the automation went live, and re-measure the new automated process a few weeks later for a fair, honest before-and-after comparison.

slides.heading: Turning Numbers Into a Simple Case Study
bullets: One paragraph: the problem
One paragraph: what you built
One paragraph: the measurable result
slides.narration: A simple case study is just three short paragraphs: what problem the client had, what you actually built to solve it, and what measurable result followed - ideally with a real time or cost number attached to that last part.

slides.heading: Getting Permission to Share Results Publicly
bullets: Always ask before using a client's name or numbers
Some clients prefer to stay anonymous - that's fine
A quick written 'yes' protects you both
slides.narration: Always ask a client's permission before sharing their name or specific numbers publicly - some are happy to be named, others prefer anonymity, and either way a quick written yes over email or chat protects you both.

modules.title: Module 5: Resume and Job Application Mastery for Automation VAs

lessons.title: Writing an Automation VA Resume

slides.heading: What Belongs on an Automation VA Resume
bullets: A clear headline naming your specialty
Specific tools you know - Zapier, Make, chatbot builders
A link to your portfolio, front and center
slides.narration: Your resume should open with a clear headline naming your specialty - "AI Automation & Chatbot VA" - list the specific tools you know like Zapier and Make by name, and put your portfolio link somewhere it can't be missed.

slides.heading: Describing Experience Without a Job History
bullets: Frame your training and mock projects as real work
Use action verbs - automated, built, streamlined
Quantify wherever you can, even mock time-savings
slides.narration: If you don't have paid experience yet, describe your training and mock projects using strong action verbs - automated, built, streamlined, integrated - and quantify what you can, like "built a lead-intake automation, cutting manual entry time by an estimated 80%."

slides.heading: Formatting for Readability
bullets: Keep it to one page
Use short bullet points, not paragraphs
Consistent, clean font and spacing
slides.narration: Keep your resume to a single page with short, scannable bullet points rather than dense paragraphs, using a clean, consistent font - a client reviewing dozens of applicants will spend only seconds per resume.

slides.heading: Common Resume Mistakes to Avoid
bullets: Vague phrases like 'automation expert' with nothing to back it up
No portfolio link at all
Listing tools you haven't actually built anything with
slides.narration: Avoid vague self-descriptions like "automation expert" with nothing to back it up, never submit a resume without your portfolio link, and never list a tool you haven't genuinely built a real workflow with.

lessons.title: Crafting Winning Proposals for Automation Gigs

slides.heading: What a Good Proposal Includes
bullets: A quick read on their specific repetitive pain point
Your specific plan - which tools, what workflow
Clear pricing and next steps
slides.narration: A strong proposal briefly identifies the specific repetitive task or bottleneck you noticed in their job post, lays out your specific plan for solving it - which tools, what workflow - and ends with clear pricing and an easy next step, like a short call.

slides.heading: Personalizing Every Proposal
bullets: Reference their actual job post or business detail
Never send an obviously copy-pasted pitch
Mention one specific automation opportunity you spotted
slides.narration: Every proposal should reference something specific from their job post or business - a tool they mentioned, a process they described - a generic copy-pasted pitch is easy to spot and easy to ignore in this specialty.

slides.heading: Structuring Your Pricing
bullets: Package by outcome - workflows built, hours saved
Offer 2-3 clear tiers, not endless options
Be upfront about ongoing tool subscription costs
slides.narration: Package your pricing around the outcome - number of workflows built, hours saved per month - and offer two or three simple tiers rather than overwhelming a client with options. Always be upfront about whether any tool subscription costs are included or separate.

slides.heading: Following Up Without Being Pushy
bullets: One polite follow-up after about a week
Add new value, don't just 'check in'
Know when to move on gracefully
slides.narration: If you don't hear back, one polite follow-up after about a week is reasonable - ideally adding something new, like a quick automation idea for their business, rather than just "checking in." If there's still no response after that, it's fine to move on gracefully.

lessons.title: Where to Find Automation & Chatbot Clients

slides.heading: Freelance Platforms
bullets: Upwork, Onlinejobs.ph, and similar sites
Filter for Zapier, Make, or automation roles
A strong profile and portfolio link matter most
slides.narration: Freelance platforms like Upwork and Onlinejobs.ph list a growing number of Zapier, Make, and general automation roles - filter specifically for those, and make sure your profile headline and portfolio link are strong.

slides.heading: Small Businesses Still Doing Everything by Hand
bullets: Many owners have never heard automation is affordable
Look for visibly manual, repetitive processes
A specific, low-pressure pitch works well
slides.narration: Many small business owners have simply never realized automation is affordable and accessible - look for businesses with visibly manual, repetitive processes, and offer a specific, low-pressure suggestion for one thing you could automate for them.

slides.heading: Referrals and Word of Mouth
bullets: Your first client is your best source of the next
Ask happy clients if they know anyone else
A short before/after case study makes referrals easier
slides.narration: Once you land one happy client, ask directly whether they know any other business owners who could use similar help - referrals convert far more easily than cold outreach, especially with a short before/after case study to share.

slides.heading: No-Code and Automation Communities
bullets: Facebook groups and forums for Zapier, Make, and no-code
Often share leads and job postings directly
Be an active, helpful member, not just a lurker
slides.narration: Facebook groups and forums built around Zapier, Make, or no-code tools generally often share leads and job postings directly, and being an active, genuinely helpful member of these communities tends to bring in the best opportunities.

lessons.title: Nailing the Discovery Call (Mapping Their Workflow Live)

slides.heading: What Clients Are Actually Evaluating
bullets: Can you understand their process quickly?
Do you ask smart, specific questions?
Do you seem trustworthy with access to their tools?
slides.narration: In a discovery call, clients aren't just checking your tool knowledge on paper - they're watching whether you can understand their process quickly, ask smart and specific questions, and seem like someone they can trust with access to their business tools.

slides.heading: Mapping Their Workflow Live on the Call
bullets: Ask them to walk through the process step by step
Sketch it back to them as they talk
This alone often impresses more than any pitch
slides.narration: Ask them to walk through their current process step by step right there on the call, and sketch a rough workflow map back to them as they talk - genuinely understanding their process in real time often impresses a client more than any prepared pitch could.

slides.heading: Talking About Pricing Confidently
bullets: Know your rate before the call, don't improvise
Explain what's included, not just the number
It's okay to say you'll follow up in writing
slides.narration: Decide your rate before the call so you're never improvising under pressure, explain clearly what's included for that price, and it's completely fine to say you'll send the full proposal in writing afterward rather than negotiating on the spot.

slides.heading: Following Up After the Call
bullets: Send a written summary within 24 hours
Attach the rough workflow map you sketched
Include your proposal or clear next steps
slides.narration: Within 24 hours of the call, send a short written summary along with the rough workflow map you sketched together, attached to your proposal or a clear next step - this reinforces that you listened closely and keeps momentum going.

modules.title: Module 6: Landing Your First Automation Client and Beyond

lessons.title: Onboarding a New Automation Client

slides.heading: What Onboarding Actually Covers
bullets: Getting access to their tools and accounts safely
Confirming the exact workflow to build first
Agreeing on the first project's scope and timeline
slides.narration: Onboarding is the process of getting properly set up with a new client: gaining safe access to the accounts and tools involved, confirming exactly which workflow you're building first, and agreeing together on the first project's scope and timeline.

slides.heading: Getting Account Access the Right Way
bullets: Ask to be added with the minimum access needed
Never ask for personal account passwords
Confirm who owns every tool and automation long-term
slides.narration: Always ask to be added with only the access level a task actually requires, rather than requesting full personal passwords - and make clear from the start that the client remains the true, permanent owner of every account and automation you build.

slides.heading: Confirming Scope Before Building Anything
bullets: Re-confirm the workflow map you agreed on
Clarify what's in scope vs a future phase
Get written sign-off before you start building
slides.narration: Re-confirm the workflow map you agreed on during the discovery call, clarify explicitly what's in scope for this first project versus a future phase, and get written sign-off before you start actually building anything.

slides.heading: Setting the First Check-In Date
bullets: Agree on when you'll show a working first version
Set expectations for how testing will happen
Clarify how and when you'll be paid
slides.narration: Agree on a date when you'll show a working first version of the automation, set expectations for how testing will happen together, and make sure payment terms - amount, method, and schedule - are clearly agreed on both sides.

lessons.title: Pricing Automation & Chatbot Projects

slides.heading: Why Clear Expectations Prevent Problems
bullets: Most client conflicts come from unspoken assumptions
A short written agreement protects you both
Revisit and adjust as workflows change
slides.narration: Most conflicts between an Automation VA and a client come from things that were never actually agreed on out loud - a short written agreement covering scope, pricing, and which tools are being used protects you both and can always be revisited.

slides.heading: Common Pricing Models
bullets: Per-project - most common for a single automation build
Monthly retainer - for ongoing maintenance and new builds
Hourly - useful early on, harder to scale long-term
slides.narration: A per-project rate is the most common model for a single automation build, a monthly retainer suits ongoing maintenance plus new workflows over time, and hourly pricing works fine early in your career but tends to be harder to scale.

slides.heading: What to Include in Your Scope of Work
bullets: Exactly which workflow(s) are included
Who pays for any tool subscriptions
What's explicitly NOT included (e.g. ongoing maintenance)
slides.narration: Your scope of work should spell out exactly which workflow or workflows are included, who pays for any ongoing tool subscriptions, and what's explicitly NOT included - like ongoing maintenance or monitoring - unless you charge separately for that.

slides.heading: Pricing Ongoing Maintenance Separately
bullets: Automations need occasional monitoring and fixes
Offer a simple monthly maintenance add-on
Be clear this is optional but recommended
slides.narration: Automations occasionally need monitoring and fixes as connected apps update - offering a simple, optional monthly maintenance add-on is a smart way to build recurring income while being upfront that it's optional but genuinely recommended.

lessons.title: Maintaining and Monitoring Automations Over Time

slides.heading: Why Automations Break Over Time
bullets: Connected apps change their features or layout
A client changes their process without telling you
API or integration changes outside anyone's control
slides.narration: Automations can break over time for reasons outside anyone's immediate control - a connected app changes its layout or features, a client quietly changes their process, or an integration is updated on the platform's end.

slides.heading: Setting Up Ongoing Monitoring
bullets: Automation platforms can alert you on failure
Do a periodic manual check even without an alert
Keep a simple log of what's running for each client
slides.narration: Configure your automation platform's built-in failure alerts, but also do a periodic manual check even when nothing has alerted you, and keep a simple running log of exactly what's live for each client so nothing gets forgotten.

slides.heading: Responding Quickly When Something Breaks
bullets: Acknowledge the issue to the client immediately
Investigate before promising a fix time
Communicate clearly once it's resolved
slides.narration: When something breaks, acknowledge the issue to the client immediately even before you know the cause, investigate before promising a specific fix time, and communicate clearly once it's actually resolved rather than leaving them wondering.

slides.heading: Reviewing and Improving Automations Periodically
bullets: Revisit each client's automations every few months
Ask if their process has changed at all
Suggest improvements proactively, don't just wait
slides.narration: Revisit each client's live automations every few months, ask whether their underlying process has changed, and proactively suggest improvements rather than only reacting when something breaks - this is what turns a one-time build into an ongoing relationship.

lessons.title: Handling Broken Automations and Client Feedback

slides.heading: Receiving Feedback Without Getting Defensive
bullets: Feedback is about the system, not you personally
Ask clarifying questions before changing anything
Thank the client for reporting issues promptly
slides.narration: It's easy to feel personally criticized when a client reports something isn't working right, but feedback is about the system, not you - ask clarifying questions before making changes, and genuinely thank clients who report issues promptly rather than letting them go unreported.

slides.heading: Diagnosing a Reported Problem Methodically
bullets: Reproduce the issue yourself before assuming a cause
Check each step of the automation in order
Don't guess - verify with the actual run history
slides.narration: Reproduce the reported issue yourself before assuming you know the cause, check each step of the automation in order using the platform's actual run history, and avoid guessing at a fix before you've verified where it actually broke.

slides.heading: Managing Scope Creep in Fixes and Changes
bullets: Define what counts as a bug fix vs a new feature
A request for new functionality isn't a 'fix'
Politely price genuinely new requests separately
slides.narration: Define clearly what counts as fixing a bug versus adding new functionality - a request for the automation to do something it was never designed to do isn't really a "fix," and it's fair to politely price that as an additional request.

slides.heading: Turning Difficult Clients Into Long-Term Ones
bullets: Most 'difficult' clients just want reliability restored quickly
Consistent, calm communication builds trust
Know when a client truly isn't the right fit
slides.narration: Many clients who seem difficult after something breaks simply want reliability restored quickly and to be kept informed - consistent, calm communication usually turns them into your most loyal clients over time.

lessons.title: Growing Your Automation VA Career

slides.heading: Leveling Up Your Skill Set
bullets: Go deeper into Make for complex, branching logic
Learn to build more advanced AI-integrated chatbots
Study basic API concepts to unlock more integrations
slides.narration: As you grow, going deeper into Make for genuinely complex logic, learning to build more advanced AI-integrated chatbots, and studying basic API concepts all let you take on higher-paying, more technically demanding projects.

slides.heading: Deciding Between More Clients or Higher Rates
bullets: More clients means more income but more maintenance
Higher rates mean the same workload, more income
Most successful Automation VAs eventually favor the second
slides.narration: At some point you'll choose between taking on more clients at your current rate, or fewer clients at a higher rate - most experienced Automation VAs eventually favor raising rates over endlessly adding more clients, since more running automations also means more ongoing maintenance.

slides.heading: Building Toward an Agency or Specialty
bullets: Some Automation VAs eventually build a small agency
Others specialize deeply in one industry's workflows
Both paths are valid - choose what fits your goals
slides.narration: Some experienced Automation VAs eventually build a small agency, bringing on other freelancers for overflow builds; others prefer staying solo and specializing deeply in one industry's specific workflows. Neither path is more "correct" - it depends on what kind of work-life you actually want.

slides.heading: Congratulations on Finishing This Training
bullets: You've covered the full Automation VA skillset
You have a portfolio, resume, and pricing plan
Time to start applying with confidence
slides.narration: Congratulations - you've now covered the full AI Automation & Chatbot VA skillset, from Zapier and Make to workflow mapping, chatbot design, portfolio-building, and long-term growth. You're ready to start applying and pitching with real confidence.
